cues.text: A Church Facing Its First Crisis
Within two decades of Pentecost, the young Church confronted a dispute that threatened to split it along the very line the Gospel was meant to cross: the boundary between Jew and Gentile.
As Paul and Barnabas preached successfully among the Gentiles of Antioch and Asia Minor, converts poured in who had never lived under the Law of Moses.

Some Jewish Christians — described in Acts as belonging to "the sect of the Pharisees" who had believed — insisted that these Gentile converts must be circumcised and required to keep the Mosaic Law in order to be saved.
The controversy was serious enough that the church at Antioch dispatched Paul, Barnabas, and others to Jerusalem to lay the question before the Apostles and elders.
The Gathering in Jerusalem
What followed, described in Acts chapter 15, is remembered as the first council of the Church, sometimes called the Apostolic Council.
Paul and Barnabas reported on the wonders God had worked among the Gentiles; the debate that followed was, by Luke's account, considerable before St. Peter rose to speak.
Peter reminded the assembly that God himself had already shown, through the household of Cornelius, that the Holy Spirit was given to Gentiles without circumcision.
He warned against placing on new disciples "a yoke" that the Jewish people themselves had not been able to bear.
James , presiding as head of the Jerusalem church, then proposed the council's judgment.
The Apostolic Decree
The council determined that Gentile converts were not bound to be circumcised or to observe the full Mosaic Law.
It asked of them only a small number of practical requirements meant to preserve fellowship at table between Jewish and Gentile believers.

These were: abstaining from food sacrificed to idols abstaining from blood abstaining from the meat of strangled animals avoiding unlawful marriage or unchastity This decision, recorded as a letter sent to the churches of Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia, is often called the Apostolic Decree.
It settled the immediate dispute and confirmed, at the highest level of apostolic authority, that salvation in Christ did not depend on adherence to the ceremonial Law of Moses.
Significance for the Church
The Council of Jerusalem established, in the Church's own founding generation, the pattern that would govern every ecumenical council afterward.
A disputed question is brought before the Church's shepherds, debated openly, and settled by a binding decision guided, as the letter itself states, by the Holy Spirit and the Apostles together.
It is for this reason regarded by many theologians as a forerunner or model of the twenty-one ecumenical councils that followed, beginning with Nicaea nearly three centuries later.
The council also secured the Church’s universal, multi-ethnic character from its earliest days.
This allowed the Gospel to spread among Gentile peoples without the burden of the Mosaic ceremonial law.
Paul would later defend this decision at length in his Letter to the Galatians.
